questions.q: Sort each statement by the algorithm it describes best.
items: Simplest to write, and slowest on a large list
Splits the list in half repeatedly, then merges the pieces back
Fastest of the three on a large list
Builds a sorted section at the start of the list, one item at a time
Needs extra memory to hold the sub-lists
Efficient on a list that is already nearly sorted
questions.feedback: Merge sort buys its speed with memory. Insertion sort is the one that rewards a list that is nearly in order already.

questions.q: Put the stages of a merge sort in order.
steps: Split the list in half, repeatedly, until every list has one item
Compare the first items of two lists
Merge the two lists into one sorted list
Repeat the merging until one sorted list remains
questions.feedback: Split all the way down first, then merge all the way back up.

questions.q: Explain why a merge sort needs more memory than a bubble sort.

markPoints.concept: a merge sort creates new sub-lists as it splits and merges
accept: new list|new lists|sub list|sublist|sublists|copies|extra lists|smaller lists|separate lists|another list|temporary|merged results
markPoints.exemplar: A merge sort creates new sub-lists as it splits the list up.

markPoints.concept: while a bubble sort swaps items inside the original list
accept: same list|original list|in place|within the list|inside the list|no extra memory|no extra space|list it was given
markPoints.exemplar: A bubble sort just swaps items inside the original list.

questions.example: A merge sort splits the list into sub-lists and then builds new merged lists, all of which have to be held in memory, whereas a bubble sort only ever swaps items around inside the original list.
questions.paraphrase: The merge method has to store the smaller lists it creates and the merged results, while the bubble method rearranges items within the list it was given.
questions.feedback: New lists against swapping in place.
